tactics.claim: Disqualify the wrong reader before the offer arrives — say plainly the offer is not for everyone, that it will demand something of them, and that if a stated condition is true of them they should stop reading right now.
tactics.mechanism: Naming who the offer is not for makes the reader run the qualification test on themselves; those who pass have privately argued themselves into being the right person, which is a stronger commitment than a claim handed to them, and inviting the wrong reader to leave signals a seller who is not needy.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated, not taught: 'if you know in your heart of hearts that you have already achieved everything you're capable of achieving — then please stop reading this report right now. There's nothing here that will help you.' Repeated later: 'this program is definitely NOT for everyone', 'you'll need a pretty thick skin because I'm going to tear your beloved business to shreds', 'Securing a place will NOT be cheap.' No conversion or refund figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable persuasion principle with an honest form here (natural deodorant genuinely is not for someone who wants sweat stopped), but the exact tactic is already recorded verbatim in marketing-conversion-copy-angles with the same quoted lines and score.

tactics.rejectReason: Already recorded in marketing-conversion-copy-angles ('Disqualify the wrong reader up front') from this same report, quoting these same lines; re-adopting would duplicate a rule and degrade skill triggering.

tactics.claim: Give the reader a numbered list of concrete symptoms with a scoring threshold ('if six or more of these sound like you, the diagnosis is clear') so they diagnose themselves.
tactics.mechanism: A conclusion the reader reaches by tallying their own behaviour cannot be argued with, and the item-by-item tally forces active engagement while converting an abstract problem into recognisable specifics.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated rather than taught — the twelve-item 'Leisure Phobia' checklist with a stated six-item threshold, followed by a list of named 'conditions' and a shorter self-question stack. No performance data.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of an existing entry in marketing-conversion-copy-angles, including the scored-threshold detail and the honest RSC translation.

tactics.claim: Substantiate the problem with cited third-party research — named academics, universities and government figures — rather than only asserting the problem is real.
tactics.mechanism: Institutional and academic sources carry authority the seller cannot manufacture, and because the citation supports the problem rather than the product, it buys credibility without the seller having to substantiate anything about what they sell.
tactics.evidence: Tim Kasser at Knox College on work hours and life satisfaction; Robert Shiller of Yale on attention; a British government figure on email time versus time with children; a 1969 workload comparison; an unsourced 80%-of-businesses-fail figure and an HP/Canon revenue figure. Named but unlinked, several figures unattributed.

rscFit.reasoning: The compliance-safe form (cite research on why baking soda irritates skin, or why the transition period happens, rather than about the product) is genuinely useful on the PDP and A+ blocks — but it is already recorded at 5/10 in marketing-conversion-copy-angles from this same report, with the same citations and the same compliance argument.

tactics.rejectReason: Already adopted in marketing-conversion-copy-angles ('substantiate the problem itself with cited third-party research'), sourced from this report and listing these same Kasser/Shiller/government citations.

tactics.claim: Stop investing in potential (talent, knowledge, commitment, effort) and instead find and eliminate the single binding constraint, because actual output is set by the weakest link rather than by the strongest inputs.
tactics.mechanism: Throughput is capped by the weakest link, so effort spent on a non-binding input produces literally zero additional output — the pizza kitchen doubles dough and topping output while the ten-pie-per-hour oven leaves the extra pizzas rotting on the floor. Once the constraint is named, the solution is usually obvious and previously wasted work converts into investment.
tactics.evidence: The pizza-parlour worked illustration and weakest-link analogy, plus Jay Abraham foreword anecdotes: no capital or credit at 18 solved by partnering with people who had both; a radio Per-Inquiry constraint solved by rephrasing the ask, claimed to yield 1,000 stations and $13M; Entrepreneur Magazine subscriptions up nine-fold in nine months; Investment Rarities sales multiplied 1,667x. Self-reported, unverified.

rscFit.reasoning: The principle is exactly right here — retention, not traffic or copy, is the measured binding constraint — but marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 1 already owns constraint-naming and already cites both the pizza-parlour illustration and these Jay Abraham foreword anecdotes in its evidence.

tactics.rejectReason: Verbatim duplicate of Step 1 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis, which already cites this report as its source.

tactics.claim: Assume the visible pain is not where the constraint sits — the pain of a constraint is felt downstream of it, so read a cluster of symptoms the way a doctor reads them and fix the underlying cause rather than patching each symptom.
tactics.mechanism: The pizza owner sees idle prep staff and turned-away customers, which is where it hurts; the oven, where the cap actually is, looks fine. Patching visible symptoms individually is Whack-a-Mole — each patch spawns new symptoms because the constraint producing them is untouched — so money is spent without moving throughput at all.
tactics.evidence: The pizza-parlour illustration, the Frank Kern anecdote (weeks lost hunting membership software when the real constraint was believing he needed it, reportedly resolved with 2,000 trial signups in 65 minutes), a medical aspirin-vs-diagnosis analogy, a Deming quote, and an unsourced 'studies have shown 90 percent of the time the real culprit is a hidden constraint in the system, not the people'.

rscFit.reasoning: Correct diagnosis discipline and directly applicable (visible pain is thin Shopify revenue; the measured constraint is the 18–22.5% repeat rate) — but marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 1 already carries the pain-displacement diagnostic word for word, with the Frank Kern anecdote, the Whack-a-Mole framing, the medical analogy and the Deming quote in its evidence.

tactics.rejectReason: Already recorded verbatim in Step 1 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis; re-adopting would create two entries competing to trigger on the same diagnostic task.

tactics.claim: Search for the constraint in three named categories — rational (errors in your thinking), procedural (counterproductive work processes) and self-imposed (rules that exist only in your head) — and specifically write down the self-imposed rules and ask which you would discard for an explosion of sales.
tactics.mechanism: Each constraint type hides differently: a thinking error looks like a requirement, a bad process feels natural because it mirrors your personality, and a self-imposed rule feels like a principle rather than a decision. Naming the categories forces a search in places an unstructured audit misses.
tactics.evidence: Illustrative self-imposed rules ('I'll never ask friends or family for money', 'I'll never market my product like that guy does') plus Schefren's claim that dropping the assumption he needed front-end products, back-end products and JV networks let Strategic Profits do $3.5M in week one and $7.4M in year one on a free report plus a back-end product. Self-reported, unverified; the part 5 restatement is a summary bullet list with no new evidence.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable diagnostic principle, age irrelevant — but marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 2 is exactly this rule, sourced from this same report, including the Strategic Profits evidence and the RSC-specific guardrail that surviving rules must be re-derived from landed cost rather than habit.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of Step 2 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis, already sourced from this report.

tactics.claim: When your list is too small to trade on parity with a big list owner, the real constraint is that you haven't courted them — pay in another currency by befriending them at industry events or asking to interview them in a way that flatters them and helps them promote their own products.
tactics.mechanism: Large list owners value attention, status and reusable content more than reciprocal list access, so a party with almost no audience can still buy exposure with hours, a flattering feature, or a genuine relationship.
tactics.evidence: Assertion with two described paths (conference friendships, flattering interviews). No named cases, no conversion or partnership figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Directly relevant to a sub-1,000-subscriber brand with nothing to trade, but already carried as an explicit refinement in marketing-acquisition-channel-selection at 5/10, sourced to this same excerpt, with the RSC translation (interview adjacent small-brand founders) and caps already written down.

tactics.rejectReason: Already recorded as a refinement in marketing-acquisition-channel-selection from this same excerpt.

tactics.claim: Silver Bullet #1 — do it wrong fast: as soon as you have an initial grounding in a strategy or tactic, apply it even if you get it wrong, because action creates clarity and more study does not.
tactics.mechanism: The information environment supplies directly contradictory expert instructions (always use a squeeze page / never use one), so no amount of additional reading can adjudicate between them — only your own test can. Prudence therefore decays into procrastination, and the money to buy the next course runs out before the 'if onlys' do.
tactics.evidence: Assertion plus a two-group taxonomy (appliers vs planners), the contradictory-guru examples, and unsupported psychologising. No data.

tactics.rejectReason: Already adopted as the apply-immediately corollary in marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 1, cited to this excerpt.

tactics.claim: Treat the absence of fast, frequent response data as a constraint in its own right and fix it by instrumenting the store — real-time analytics, session/visitor recording and on-site surveys — then change the page based on what you observe rather than on the plan you wrote last month.
tactics.mechanism: Without observation you are guessing at why visitors do not buy, so you optimize whatever you happen to believe, and you cannot double down on a winner or kill a loser before it drains the bank. Watching real sessions and asking visitors directly surfaces the specific confusion, missing information or friction that no amount of internal reasoning produces — and it does so as qualitative evidence, which does not require statistical volume to be informative.
tactics.evidence: Named as Silver Bullet #2 in overview, then detailed later with tool name-drops (Woopra for real-time analytics, ClickTale for session recording, 4q.iperceptions for on-page survey) and the claim that today's reports are graphically robust enough that 'a sixth-grader could understand them'. No account data, no before/after, no instrumentation procedure.

The practice itself is free and solo-executable today (Microsoft Clarity or similar for recordings, a one-question exit survey on the Shopify PDP) and lands on the ~$875/mo Shopify side where CRO work is live and the tracking gate is open. Its real value is that qualitative feedback is readable at ~54 orders/month where a quantitative funnel report is not: twenty session recordings show a broken variant picker or an unanswered transition-period question even though no conversion-rate delta would ever reach significance. Held at 6 because Amazon — the larger ~$1,800/mo channel — cannot be instrumented this way at all, it produces diagnosis rather than revenue, and marketing-conversion-friction-audit already tells you what to look for once you are looking.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-friction-audit

tactics.claim: Treat the plan as a starting trajectory rather than a detailed plan and revise it continuously on market feedback, because most successful companies ended up somewhere other than where they planned and the ones that scaled before finding the right model are the ones that died.
tactics.mechanism: Markets and technology change faster than plans, so executing yesterday's plan guarantees a mismatch; a loose destination permits tactical flexibility, while scaling spend on an unvalidated model turns burn rate into 'the cancer that kills the business'.
tactics.evidence: Fred Wilson / Union Square Ventures portfolio data (companies that did not change their model after funding were 500% more likely to fail; those that changed were 50% more likely to return 500%), a 'Founders at Work' quote about PayPal, Excite and Flickr pivoting, an unsourced '80% of new businesses fail within five years' figure and an HP/Canon revenue statistic. Secondhand statistics, no methodology given.

tactics.evidence: Assertion only; no study, no case, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Motivational self-diagnosis with no mechanism that touches a product page, listing, email flow or campaign.

tactics.claim: Stop treating conversion rate as the metric to maximize — a falling conversion rate alongside rising traffic is fine, because the goal is total conversions and unfamiliar new visitors convert at a lower percentage before later becoming buyers.
tactics.mechanism: Conversion rate is a ratio whose denominator you are deliberately trying to grow; widening the top of the funnel admits colder prospects, so the percentage drops while absolute orders rise. Optimizing the ratio therefore incentivizes shrinking the audience.
tactics.evidence: Assertion, framed as heresy he expects pushback on. No account data.

rscFit.reasoning: Correct and durable, but marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 7 already owns exactly this — read an unusually high conversion rate as a narrow-funnel symptom, expect the rate to fall as the top widens, optimize total sales rather than the percentage — parked at scale because at ~54 orders/month a rate movement is noise.

tactics.claim: Before setting up or reading any metrics, answer a fixed question list — what data would help me reach my current goal faster, what is the visitor's purpose, what steps does a visitor take to become a customer, what do I need to learn to make better marketing decisions — so measurement is scoped to a decision.
tactics.mechanism: Analytics generate unlimited data; defining the decision first means you collect and read only the data that could change an action, instead of drowning in reports that inform nothing.

tactics.claim: Map the seven-step buying process (recognize the need, research, refine and reflect, reach out to other buyers, resolve, purchase, reconsider) and match a different message and asset to each step.
tactics.mechanism: Buying is a process rather than an event and the prospect's needs evolve through it; a message aimed at the wrong step talks past them, while a message matched to their current step moves them forward rather than interrupting them.
tactics.evidence: The seven steps enumerated with a suggested emphasis for each (frame the need early, benefits at research, premiums/guarantee/price incentives at refine, third-party opinion at reach out, trust logos at resolve, thank-you page at purchase, guarantee reassurance at reconsider). Assertion and taxonomy, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable but wholly covered piece by piece and more usefully: marketing-awareness-level-messaging owns the awareness ladder, marketing-problem-solution-inventory the before/during/after sequence, marketing-offer-construction guarantee and bonus placement, marketing-conversion-friction-audit trust markers at decision points, marketing-lifecycle-email-flows cart abandonment, and marketing-post-purchase-onboarding the confirmation window.

tactics.claim: Before deciding, prospects leave your site to check consumer-generated media — user reviews, blogs, discussion forums — and trust those opinions more than your advertising copy, so monitor what is being said about you there and make sure nothing derogatory stands without a rebuttal.
tactics.mechanism: Third-party accounts are read as disinterested, so they outrank seller claims in the buyer's evaluation; an unanswered negative account off your own property therefore does more damage than any on-page copy can repair, and a visible, reasonable response neutralizes it for every later reader of the same thread.
tactics.evidence: A cited Deloitte & Touche survey claiming more than 80% of people who seek out these opinions believe them more than advertising copy. Secondhand citation, no link, no figures on the effect of responding.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable trust-and-proof principle whose described behaviour has only intensified since 2008. Genuinely additive: marketing-review-mining owns extracting language from reviews you already have and choosing which to display, and the voice-of-customer agent already mines Reddit and Judge.me monthly, but nothing owns the response side — replying to a negative Amazon review on the ~$1,800/mo channel, or answering a 'has anyone tried this brand' thread in a sensitive-skin or zero-waste subreddit. Free, purely editorial, solo-executable, and it lands on the exact objections (baking soda burned, quit by noon, gave up during the transition) that drive the 18–22.5% repeat rate. Held at 6 because it protects trust rather than producing revenue, it will never be measurable at this volume, and it carries a hard guardrail: Amazon permits a seller response to a review but prohibits anything that reads as review manipulation, and forum participation must be disclosed as the brand rather than posted as a customer.

targetSkill.name: marketing-review-mining
targetSkill.description: Add the response side of review work: monitor off-site consumer-generated media (Amazon reviews, subreddits, forums) where buyers verify you, and leave no material negative account standing without a reasonable, disclosed brand reply — with guardrails on Amazon review-manipulation policy and forum self-promotion disclosure.

tactics.claim: Counter buyer's remorse immediately after the order: re-sell the buyer on the benefits of what they just bought, restate the money-back guarantee, and tell them how to reach you if a question arises.
tactics.mechanism: Doubt forms in the minutes and hours after payment — did I need this, can I afford it — and an unanswered doubt turns into a refund or a cancellation. Most buyers only need to know the money-back option exists rather than to use it, so restating the guarantee removes the risk without costing anything, and re-stating the benefits gives the decision a reason to survive the doubt.
tactics.evidence: Assertion within the seventh buying-process step, plus the observation that 'most buyers simply need the reassurance that they can get their money back if need be'. No refund or retention figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable retention psychology, free, and aimed at the binding constraint — repeat customers are 45–52% of revenue and the churn event is a first-time buyer deciding during the transition period that the product failed. marketing-post-purchase-onboarding already owns the first-48-hours promise schedule and the pre-arrival education series, and marketing-offer-construction owns writing and placing the guarantee on the PDP; the additive part is narrow but real — the guarantee should be restated inside the order-confirmation and first post-purchase email, not only on the page that sold them, and that email should re-sell the specific benefit rather than just confirm shipping. Capped at 5 for that overlap and because at ~54 orders/month a change in refund rate will never be readable. Note the tension with the fear-handling rule in marketing-conversion-copy-angles: the guarantee restatement is evidence, but bare 'don't worry' reassurance is not, so the same email still owes the dated transition timeline.

targetSkill.name: marketing-post-purchase-onboarding
targetSkill.description: Add a remorse-countering step to the first post-purchase touch: restate the money-back guarantee and re-sell the specific benefit inside the order confirmation and first email, alongside the dated transition timeline, rather than leaving the guarantee only on the page that sold them.

tactics.claim: At the resolution stage add credentialing trust logos (e.g. Hackersafe) and recover form abandonment, because the buyer has decided but has not yet completed the transaction.
tactics.mechanism: Deciding to buy and actually buying are separate events, and the gap between them is where cart and form abandonment happen; security credentials plus abandonment recovery close that gap.
tactics.evidence: Assertion, with shopping-cart abandonment rates offered as proof the gap exists. No conversion figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Both halves are already owned — marketing-conversion-friction-audit requires at least one credibility marker at every decision point, explicitly naming secure-checkout badges beside the button, and marketing-lifecycle-email-flows owns the abandoned-cart flow already live in this account.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of existing rules, and the named badge is fast-decaying platform mechanics (Hackersafe became McAfee Secure and then largely disappeared as a trust signal).

tactics.claim: Influence is highest at the earliest stage, before the prospect has framed their own need — so help them frame the problem in a way that projects your strengths and minimizes your weaknesses, rather than waiting until they are comparing products on price and features.
tactics.mechanism: A buyer who has not yet defined what a good solution looks like will adopt the definition offered to them; whoever supplies the evaluation criteria first shapes every later comparison, because the shortlist is filtered against those criteria. Once the prospect has built their own criteria from competitors' messaging, you are arguing against a frame instead of setting one.
tactics.evidence: Assertion within the first buying-process step, with the added claim that framing the need also lays the foundation for a long-term relationship. No examples, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable positioning principle, free and purely editorial. The honest form here is concrete: a 'how to choose a natural deodorant that actually works' education piece or A+ block that establishes baking-soda irritation and surviving the transition as the criteria a buyer should judge on, written before they compare Native and Dr. Squatch on scent and price. Capped at 5 because it substantially overlaps three recorded rules — the 'how do I pick' solution-aware stem and the market-image bridge in marketing-awareness-level-messaging, and the us-vs-them attribute cap in marketing-product-image-stack. The additive part is narrow: those govern the comparison surface, this says the criteria should be set upstream in problem-aware content before comparison begins. Any criterion named must be a defensible formulation fact under the body-care claim rules, and at ~54 orders/month the effect will be judged rather than measured.

targetSkill.name: marketing-awareness-level-messaging
targetSkill.description: Add a criteria-setting rule for problem-aware content: supply the evaluation criteria upstream, before the prospect builds their own from competitor messaging, so later comparisons are filtered against attributes you win on — with the constraint that every criterion must be a defensible formulation fact.

tactics.claim: Solve a recurring problem permanently by running it through a fixed sequence — identify the problem, reframe it from a person to a system, probe with specific questions, name the real constraint, state the outcome you wanted, complete the sentence 'the solution is to install a system that…', design that system, then implement it.
tactics.mechanism: A one-off fix repairs an instance while leaving the process that produced it intact, so the problem recurs and consumes attention indefinitely. Forcing the answer into the form 'install a system that…' converts a repair into a documented process, and each such process permanently removes a category of problem from the operator's plate, which is what frees capacity to grow.
tactics.evidence: An eight-step procedure worked through on a single hypothetical (hiring an incompetent employee → the real constraint is the absence of a hiring and training system), plus a ten-item sub-checklist (A–J) for designing the system. No business outcome data, no named case.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable process-design principle and free. Roughly half does not transfer — steps on staffing, accountabilities, non-compliance enforcement and employee notification presuppose people who do not exist here, and the worked example is a hiring problem for a solo operator with no team. What transfers is the terminal instruction: when a marketing problem recurs, the output is a written process, not another fix. Real recurrences here are concrete — a deodorant SKU stocking out (which caps everything downstream and no marketing work repairs), a post-purchase flow silently breaking, listing copy drifting out of sync across 12 SKUs and two channels, review requests never going out. A checklist file costs an hour and prevents the recurrence. Capped at 5 because the first three steps duplicate Step 1 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis and the sequencing duplicates Step 3, the evidence is one hypothetical, and it protects hours rather than producing revenue.

tactics.claim: Log one full week in 15-minute increments, compute your productivity rate, then cut your total work hours to (productive hours ÷ 0.8) so you are forced to an 80% productivity rate, and only add hours back once the faster pace has become your default.
tactics.mechanism: You have conditioned yourself to work at a low productivity rate and available hours absorb the slack; artificially constraining the hours creates pressure that forces prioritisation and eliminates low-value activity, so output per hour rises and can then be scaled back up at the new rate.
tactics.evidence: Worked arithmetic on a hypothetical 'Bob' (50 hours at work, 10 productive, therefore cut to 12.5 hours over five days), plus attribution of 'work velocity' to Bill Gates and the 80% target to blogger Steve Pavlina. Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: A personal time-management regimen with no marketing surface: it never touches a product page, Amazon listing, email flow, offer, or the $30/day Meta campaign. The one adjacent question — where a solo operator's finite hours should land — is already owned by marketing-performance-pattern-analysis.

tactics.rejectReason: Not a marketing tactic; adding a 'cut your hours to 12.5' rule to a marketing skill would also damage triggering, since skill descriptions are how Claude Code selects skills.

tactics.claim: Finish one project and get revenue flowing from it before starting the next, rather than running several concurrently, because profit accrues from completion dates and serialising the same total work triples the profit-weeks earned.
tactics.mechanism: Work-in-progress earns nothing; only a finished project earns. Running three projects concurrently pushes all three completion dates toward the end of the window so each earns for only a few weeks, while doing them one at a time in the same total hours lets the first complete early and earn throughout.
tactics.evidence: Two Gantt-style diagrams (ABC/ABC/ABC finishing at weeks 7/8/9 = 3 profit-weeks, versus AAA/BBB/CCC finishing at weeks 3/6/9 = 9 profit-weeks) and a claimed '300% more profit'. Illustrative arithmetic only, no account data.

rscFit.reasoning: Sound and genuinely relevant to a solo operator juggling a live $30/day Meta campaign, an unwritten post-entry email sequence, an unbuilt subscribe-and-save cadence and a PDP that wants a results timeline — but already in the fleet.

tactics.rejectReason: Step 3 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis carries this exact rule, cited to this exact excerpt, with the same Gantt illustration, the same 300% figure and the same 'pick the one likeliest to make the most money soonest' selection criterion.

tactics.claim: Divide your week like a professional athlete into three distinct modes — prime project days on the single highest-leverage project, preparation and commitment days for routine tasks, and at least 24 hours of total relaxation with no work contact.
tactics.mechanism: Roughly 20% of what you do produces 80% of results, so the decisive moments are few; burnout degrades your state exactly when a high-leverage opportunity appears. Segregating deep work, admin and full recovery builds mental capacity the way training/practice/game segregation builds physical capacity.
tactics.evidence: Attributed to Dan Sullivan, plus the author's description of his own schedule and a claim that trying it for two to three weeks will hook you for life. No figures, no case.

tactics.rejectReason: A manufactured 'I swore I'd never do this again' framing on a $12 consumable is the dishonest end of the reason-why rule already recorded, and there is no real broken commitment to point at.

tactics.claim: Report how much labour went into producing the thing ('seven long months', 'more time, research and effort than all my previous six reports combined') as proof of its value.
tactics.mechanism: Visible effort invested signals value and justifies both the price and the reader's attention, because a thing that cost a lot to make is presumed to be worth a lot to receive.
tactics.evidence: Two statements in the lead about research duration and effort relative to prior reports. Self-reported, unverified.

rscFit.reasoning: The honest ecommerce form — small-batch, made by one person, the founder's reason for formulating it — is already owned by the provenance half of the identification-material audit in marketing-awareness-level-messaging and by the four-jobs test for physical detail in marketing-problem-solution-inventory.

tactics.rejectReason: Nothing additive, and 'seven months of research' has no defensible analogue for a deodorant formulation without becoming an unsupportable claim.

tactics.claim: Paint the cost of not acting — burnout, bankruptcy, damaged health, a broken marriage, children who grow up while you work.
tactics.mechanism: Fear and avoidance language cuts through where benefit language blends in, and naming the feared outcome proves you understand the stakes.
tactics.evidence: Several pages of consequence painting, supported by cited polls, the Kasser study and government figures. No performance data on the framing itself.

rscFit.reasoning: marketing-conversion-copy-angles already carries negative framing at 6/10, the 'pitfall warning' verbalization transform, and the fear-handling rule that governs how to put the fear back down.

tactics.rejectReason: Adds no mechanism, and the register — life-ruining consequences — badly overshoots a $12 consumable at a $50.46 AOV where the honest fear is a ruined shirt.

tactics.claim: Concede the offer can fail, then define the only two failure modes as the reader's own — not reading carefully and not implementing.
tactics.mechanism: Conceding fallibility reads as candour and raises credibility, while pre-assigning the failure to the buyer removes the seller's exposure and pre-empts a refund argument.
tactics.evidence: 'So could Rich's findings actually fail to multiply YOUR income? Shockingly, yes. But only if you: 1) Fail to read this report carefully and 2) Fail to put the advice intelligently to work.' Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: The legitimate part — stating the condition under which the product will not deliver — is already owned by the disqualification and admit-flaws rules in marketing-conversion-copy-angles.

tactics.rejectReason: The additive part actively conflicts with an adopted rule: pre-blaming the buyer is the inverse of the blame-absolution rule this catalogue relies on at the week-two churn point, and 'it failed because you didn't use it right' is precisely the belief driving the 18–22.5% repeat rate. It is also close to unusable against a 30-day money-back guarantee.
